lines: Workers paint a giant leaking tank brown to hide the drips.
The tank stands by Boston Harbor, fifty feet tall.
It holds up to two point three million gallons of molasses.
Neighbors even collect the leaking syrup for their homes.
Each time the tank is filled, it groans.
The man in charge, Arthur Jell, has no engineering experience.
He never fills it with water to test for leaks.
In January 1919, a ship pumps in warm molasses.
The next day, the air warms up fast.
At half past noon, the tank bursts.
Its rivets shoot out like machine gun fire.
A wave twenty-five feet high rushes out at thirty-five miles per hour.
It sweeps buildings off their foundations.
It tips a streetcar off its tracks.
You see, it's like warm honey. Heat it, and it runs fast. Let it cool, and it turns thick.
Molasses gets thinner when it is warm or pushed hard.
So the wave races out fast.
Then it hits the winter cold and turns thick as glue.
People are trapped in the sticky mass.
Twenty-one people die.
Later, experts found the steel was only half as thick as it should have been.
The leaks were painted over. The smell of molasses stayed for decades.

claims.claim: When filled with molasses, the tank leaked so badly that it was painted brown to hide the leakage; local residents collected leaked molasses for their homes.
The tank, adjacent to Boston Harbor, stood 50 feet tall and held as much as 2.3 million US gallons of molasses.

Arthur Jell, who had no architectural or engineering experience, neglected basic safety tests such as filling the tank with water to check for leaks, and ignored groaning noises each time it was filled.
The day before the January 15, 1919 disaster, a ship delivered a fresh load of warmed molasses; temperatures climbed rapidly.
The tank collapsed at about 12:30 p.m.; witnesses heard a sound like a machine gun as the rivets shot out.
A wave of molasses 25 feet high moved at 35 mph, swept buildings off their foundations and tipped a streetcar off its tracks.
Molasses thins and flows quickly under pressure and heat; it then cooled and thickened, trapping victims.
A 2014 investigation found the steel was half as thick as it should have been; residents reported the area smelled of molasses for decades.
